sections.title: What is Time & Space Complexity?
sections.content:
When you write an algorithm, two questions immediately follow: **how long will it take to run**, and **how much memory will it use**? The naive answer is to benchmark it - run the code and measure. But benchmarking is hardware-dependent. The same program runs in 2 seconds on your laptop and 0.2 seconds on a server. We need a **hardware-independent measure** of how an algorithm behaves - that measure is complexity analysis.

The key insight is that we don't care about the exact time. We care about **how the time grows as the input grows**. Imagine searching for a name in a phonebook. If you flip through every page from the start, a 1000-page phonebook takes 1000 steps and a 2000-page book takes 2000 steps - time grows linearly with input size. If you use binary search (open to the middle, discard half), a 1000-page book takes ~10 steps and a 2000-page book takes ~11 steps - time grows logarithmically. The difference is dramatic at scale.

**Time complexity** measures how the number of operations grows as input size `n` grows. **Space complexity** measures how much extra memory is consumed as `n` grows. Both are expressed using **Big-O notation**, which captures the worst-case growth rate, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.

Complexity analysis is the language interviewers use when they ask 'can you do better?' It's also the tool you use to decide between approaches before writing a single line of code. A solution that looks elegant but is O(n²) on a 10⁵ input will time-out - knowing this upfront saves hours of debugging.

sections.title: When to Think About Complexity
sections.content: You should be thinking about complexity from the moment you read a problem. Check the constraint on `n` first - it tells you what complexity class your solution must fall in. An interviewer asking 'can you do better?' is a direct signal to analyze your current solution's complexity and find a more efficient approach. When your brute-force solution gets a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) verdict on an online judge, complexity analysis tells you why and what class you need to reach.
signals: Interviewer asks 'what is the time complexity of your solution?'
Brute force passes small test cases but TLEs on large ones
Constraint n ≤ 10^5 (hints O(n log n) or O(n) max)
Constraint n ≤ 20 (O(2^n) or O(n!) might be fine)
'Can you solve this in O(1) space?' or 'in-place?'
Comparing two approaches and choosing the better one
Deciding if an extra data structure is worth its memory cost

sections.title: Big-O Notation
sections.content:
**Big-O notation** formally describes an upper bound on an algorithm's growth rate. `O(f(n))` means: for large enough `n`, the algorithm's cost is at most some constant multiple of `f(n)`. We drop constants and lower-order terms because at large scale, they're irrelevant - `O(2n)` and `O(n)` are both just `O(n)`.

## Common Complexity Classes

| Notation | Name | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Constant | Same cost regardless of input size. Array index access. |
| O(log n) | Logarithmic | Input halves at each step. Binary search. |
| O(n) | Linear | Visit every element once. Linear scan. |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | Sort the input. Merge sort, heap sort. |
| O(n²) | Quadratic | Every pair of elements. Nested loops over same array. |
| O(2^n) | Exponential | Every subset. Brute-force recursion on subsets. |
| O(n!) | Factorial | Every permutation. Brute-force traveling salesman. |

## Dominant Terms

When an algorithm has cost `3n² + 5n + 100`, the dominant term is `n²`. As `n` grows, `n²` overwhelms everything else. So we write O(n²). The rules: keep only the fastest-growing term, drop constants.

## Growth Rate Comparison

For `n = 1000`: O(log n) ≈ 10 ops, O(n) = 1000 ops, O(n log n) ≈ 10,000 ops, O(n²) = 1,000,000 ops, O(2^n) = astronomically large.

sections.title: Deriving Complexity from Code
sections.content:
**Reading code for complexity** is a skill you develop by practice. Here are the rules:

## Loops

A single loop from `0` to `n` → O(n). A loop from `0` to `n` that increments by doubling (`i *= 2`) → O(log n) because input is halved each step. Two nested loops both from `0` to `n` → O(n²). But watch out: if the inner loop runs from `i` to `n` (not `0` to `n`), it's still O(n²) asymptotically - it's `n*(n-1)/2` which is O(n²).

## Recursion

For recursion, write a **recurrence relation**. Binary search calls itself on half the input and does O(1) work: `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)`. Solving this gives O(log n). Merge sort splits in half and does O(n) merge work: `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)`, which gives O(n log n) by the Master Theorem.

## Space Complexity

Space complexity counts **auxiliary memory** you allocate. Creating an array of size `n` → O(n) space. A recursive function that calls itself `n` times deep → O(n) stack space even if no other memory is used. An in-place algorithm that only uses a few variables → O(1) space.

## The Shortcut

Count the nested loops that depend on `n`. One loop = O(n). Two nested = O(n²). One loop where the variable doubles/halves = O(log n). Then add recursion stack space if applicable.

sections.title: Complexity Cheat Sheet (Code Pattern Reference)
sections.explanation: This template maps common code patterns to their complexity class. Use it as a reference when reading code - identify which pattern a loop/recursion matches, then assign its Big-O immediately.

items.name: Amortized Analysis
items.description: Some operations are expensive occasionally but cheap on average over many calls. A dynamic array's `push` is usually O(1) but triggers O(n) copy when capacity doubles. However, the copy cost is spread over all pushes - amortized O(1) per push. When interviewers say 'amortized O(1)' they mean this averaging over a sequence of operations.

items.name: Best / Average / Worst Case
items.description: Big-O usually describes worst case, but sometimes we distinguish. QuickSort is O(n²) worst case (already-sorted input with bad pivot) but O(n log n) average case with random pivot. Interviewers sometimes ask for all three. In practice, average case matters more for randomized algorithms.

items.name: Space-Time Tradeoff
items.description: You can often trade memory for speed. Caching computed results (memoization) increases space from O(1) to O(n) but drops time from O(2^n) to O(n). Precomputing a prefix sum array costs O(n) space but reduces every range query from O(n) to O(1). Recognizing this tradeoff is a core interview skill.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: Analyzing complexity is a meta-operation - reading each line of code once costs O(1) per line. The total analysis time is proportional to the size of the code, not the size of the input `n`. You are not running the algorithm; you are reasoning about it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting recursion stack space: a function that recurses `n` levels deep uses O(n) space even if no arrays are created. DFS on a skewed tree has O(n) stack space, not O(1).
Treating O(2n) as different from O(n): constants are always dropped in Big-O. O(2n), O(5n), and O(n) are all the same complexity class. Only the growth rate matters.

Assuming nested loops are always O(n²): if the inner loop runs from `i` to `i+k` for a fixed constant `k`, it's still O(n). If the inner loop variable is independent of the outer, examine carefully - it might be O(n * m) not O(n²).

Confusing the value of n with the size of n: in bit manipulation, the input is a number `n`, but the size of the input is `log n` bits. An algorithm that loops `n` times is O(n) in terms of the number's value but O(2^(bits)) in terms of input size - this matters in number theory problems.

Ignoring the cost of built-in operations: `array.splice(i, 1)` is O(n) not O(1) because it shifts elements. `string += char` in a loop is O(n²) total due to string immutability. Assuming all JS array methods are O(1) leads to hidden quadratic solutions.

items.title: Two Sum
items.why: Forces you to compare O(n²) brute force vs O(n) hash map solution - the complexity difference is the entire lesson.

items.title: Binary Search
items.why: The canonical O(log n) algorithm - understanding why halving gives logarithmic complexity is foundational.

items.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
items.why: Requires analyzing O(nk) naive vs O(n log k) heap solution - complexity analysis drives the algorithm choice.

items.title: Maximum Subarray
items.why: Contrast O(n²) brute force (all subarrays) with O(n) Kadane's - demonstrates how algorithmic insight collapses complexity.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Basic math topics like modular arithmetic and prime sieves come with their own complexity stories - O(√n) for trial division, O(n log log n) for Sieve - applying complexity analysis to concrete math algorithms reinforces the framework you just learned.
